definition: Azure's free hub for moving an estate: an on-site appliance discovers servers, databases and web apps and collects performance data; assessments give readiness, right-sized targets and cost estimates, plus a business case; dependency analysis maps connections; and built-in tools replicate and cut over servers, with database and web app migration alongside.
example: Six weeks of Azure Migrate discovery found 30 unused VMs and showed the rest could run on about 40% less compute.

definition: The route chosen for each workload in a migration - retire, retain, rehost (lift and shift), replatform onto managed services, refactor or rearchitect, or replace with SaaS - trading speed against benefit. With a deadline, migrate first and modernise second, replatforming where it is cheap and refactoring only where the gain is proven.
example: Web apps replatform to App Service, 80 VMs rehost, the warehouse is retained, and the ERP integration is replaced by a Logic Apps workflow.

definition: Discovering which servers and processes talk to which, on what ports, from real network data - agentless or agent-based in Azure Migrate. It groups servers that must move together and exposes hidden links such as hard-coded IP addresses, scheduled file transfers and licence servers before cutover rather than during it.
example: Dependency data showed the order system calling a forgotten licence server every morning; it joined the same wave.

definition: A group of workloads that depend on each other and migrate together, following a repeatable routine: replicate, test-migrate into an isolated network, cut over in an agreed window with go/no-go criteria and a rollback plan, watch closely (hypercare), then decommission the source. The first wave is a low-risk pilot.
example: Wave 1 moved three internal web apps and their shared SQL instance; wave 4 moved the order system with its licence server.

definition: Replacing a legacy system gradually: a façade such as API Management or Front Door routes each capability to either the old system or new code, capabilities are rebuilt one at a time and their routes switched, and the old system shrinks until it can be retired. Rolling back is a routing change.
example: Returns moved first from the old order system to a new service on Container Apps, by changing one API Management route.

definition: Extends Azure management to servers, Kubernetes clusters and SQL Server instances running outside Azure - on site or in other clouds - so Azure Policy, Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor, update management and RBAC apply to them too. It is how what is retained stays governed like everything else.
example: The warehouse servers stay on site but appear in Azure as Arc-enabled servers, with the same policies and patching.
